paragraphs: MADISON, with HAMILTON

The ancient confederacies I described in my last paper do not exhaust what experience can teach us on this subject. Some institutions that exist today rest on a similar principle and deserve careful study. The first to come to mind is the Germanic body.

In the early centuries of Christianity, seven separate nations lived in Germany, and they had no common chief. One of them, the Franks, conquered the Gauls and founded the kingdom that still bears their name. In the ninth century the warlike monarch Charlemagne sent his victorious armies in every direction, and Germany became part of his vast dominions. After his empire was broken up under his sons, this portion became a separate, independent empire. Charlemagne and his immediate descendants held the substance of imperial power, along with its emblems and dignity. But the chief vassals, whose fiefs had become hereditary and who sat in the national diets that Charlemagne had left in place, gradually shook off imperial control and rose to sovereign jurisdiction and independence. Imperial sovereignty was too weak to restrain such powerful dependents, or to keep the empire united and at peace. The princes and states waged the most furious private wars on one another, with every kind of calamity in their train. The imperial authority could not keep public order and declined step by step, until it was almost extinct in the anarchy that shook the long interval between the death of the last emperor of the Suabian line and the accession of the first emperor of the Austrian line. In the eleventh century the emperors held full sovereignty; by the fifteenth they had little more than the symbols and trappings of power.

From this feudal system, which itself has many of the important features of a confederacy, there grew the federal system that makes up the Germanic empire. Its powers are divided among three bodies. One is a diet, which represents the member states of the confederacy. Another is the emperor, the chief executive, who has a negative on the decrees of the diet. The third consists of the imperial chamber and the aulic council, two courts with supreme jurisdiction over controversies that concern the empire or that arise among its members.

The diet holds the general power to legislate for the empire. It may make war and peace, form alliances, assess quotas of troops and money, build fortresses, regulate coin, and admit new members. It may also place disobedient members under the ban of the empire, which strips the offender of his sovereign rights and forfeits his possessions. The members of the confederacy are expressly forbidden to make compacts that harm the empire; to impose tolls and duties on trade among themselves without the consent of the emperor and diet; to change the value of money; to wrong one another; or to give aid or refuge to disturbers of the public peace. Those who violate any of these restrictions are declared under the ban. The members of the diet, in their capacity as members, are in all cases subject to judgment by the emperor and diet, and in their private capacities by the aulic council and imperial chamber.

The emperor's prerogatives are many. The most important are these: he alone may bring proposals before the diet; he may negative its resolutions; he names ambassadors, confers dignities and titles, fills vacant electorates, and founds universities; he grants privileges, provided they do not injure the states of the empire; he receives and applies the public revenues; and in general he watches over the public safety. In certain cases the electors act as his council. As emperor he holds no territory within the empire and receives no revenue for his support. But the revenue and dominions he holds in other capacities make him one of the most powerful princes in Europe.

Seeing such an array of constitutional powers in the representatives and the head of this confederacy, one would naturally suppose that it must be an exception to the general character of similar systems. The reality is quite the opposite. The empire rests on a fundamental principle: it is a community of sovereigns, the diet represents sovereigns, and the laws are addressed to sovereigns. That principle makes the empire a body without strength, unable to govern its own members, unprotected against outside dangers, and in constant internal turmoil.

The history of Germany is one of wars between the emperor and the princes and states, and of wars among the princes and states themselves. It is a record of the strong running wild and the weak being oppressed; of foreign intrusions and foreign intrigues; of requisitions for men and money that were ignored or only partly met; of efforts to enforce them that either came to nothing or brought slaughter and desolation, in which the innocent suffered with the guilty. It is a record of general feebleness, confusion, and misery.

In the sixteenth century the emperor, with one part of the empire behind him, was seen fighting the other princes and states. In one of these conflicts the emperor himself was routed and very nearly captured by the elector of Saxony. The late king of Prussia was more than once set against his imperial sovereign, and usually got the better of him. Quarrels and wars among the members themselves have been so frequent that the German annals are full of bloody pages describing them. Before the peace of Westphalia, Germany was ravaged by a thirty years' war. The emperor and half the empire stood on one side, and Sweden and the other half on the opposite side. Peace was in the end negotiated, and dictated, by foreign powers, and its articles, to which foreign powers are parties, became a fundamental part of the Germanic constitution.

Suppose the nation is, in some emergency, more united than usual by the need to defend itself. Its situation is still wretched. Military preparations must first go through so many tedious debates, caused by the jealousies, pride, separate aims, and conflicting claims of sovereign bodies, that the enemy is already in the field before the diet can settle on its arrangements, and is retiring to winter quarters before the federal troops are ready to take the field.

The small body of national troops judged necessary in peacetime is badly kept up and poorly paid. It is infected with local prejudices and supported by uneven and disproportionate contributions to the treasury.

Because it was impossible to keep order and administer justice among these sovereign subjects, a new scheme was tried. The empire was divided into nine or ten circles or districts, each was given an internal organization, and each was charged with the military enforcement of the laws against delinquent and stubborn members. This experiment has only shown more fully the radical vice of the constitution. Every circle is a small portrait of the deformities of this political monster. The circles either fail to carry out their commissions, or they carry them out with all the devastation and carnage of civil war. Sometimes entire circles fall into default, and then they add to the very harm they were set up to cure.

We can judge how this scheme of military coercion works from an instance reported by Thuanus. In Donawerth, a free and imperial city in the circle of Suabia, the Abbe de St. Croix held certain immunities that had been reserved to him. When he exercised them on some public occasions, the townspeople committed outrages against him. As a result the city was placed under the ban of the empire, and the Duke of Bavaria, although he was director of a different circle, secured an appointment to enforce it. He soon appeared before the city with ten thousand troops. He saw a good opportunity, as he had secretly planned from the start, to revive an old claim, on the pretext that his ancestors had allowed the place to be detached from his territory.(1) He took possession of it in his own name, disarmed and punished the inhabitants, and joined the city once more to his domains.

Someone may ask what has kept this disjointed machine from collapsing altogether for so long. The answer is plain. Most of the members are weak and do not want to expose themselves to the mercy of foreign powers. Most of the principal members, too, are weak compared with the formidable powers around them. The emperor draws great weight and influence from his own separate, hereditary dominions, and he has an interest in preserving a system tied to his family pride and making him the first prince of Europe. These causes sustain a feeble and precarious Union—while the repellent quality that goes with the nature of sovereignty, and that grows stronger with time, blocks any reform based on proper consolidation. And even if this obstacle could be overcome, we should not imagine that the neighboring powers would allow a revolution that gave the empire the force and preeminence it is entitled to. Foreign nations have long regarded themselves as having a stake in the changes that events bring to this constitution, and on various occasions they have shown that their policy is to perpetuate its anarchy and weakness.

If more direct examples were needed, Poland, as a government over local sovereigns, could fairly be mentioned. No proof could show more strikingly the calamities that flow from such institutions. Unfit for self-government and for self-defense alike, Poland has long been at the mercy of its powerful neighbors, who recently had the mercy to relieve it of a third of its people and territory.
The tie among the Swiss cantons hardly amounts to a confederacy, although it is sometimes cited as an example of how stable such institutions can be.
They have no common treasury; no common troops, even in war; no common coin; no common court; and no other common mark of sovereignty.

What holds them together is the peculiar lie of their land; their individual weakness and insignificance; fear of powerful neighbors, to one of which they were once subject; the few causes of quarrel among a people with such simple and uniform manners; their joint interest in their dependent possessions; the mutual aid they need to put down insurrections and rebellions, which is expressly promised and often called for and given; and the need for some regular and permanent way of settling disputes among the cantons. The provision is that the parties to a dispute each choose four judges from the neutral cantons, and if these disagree, they choose an umpire. This tribunal, bound by an oath of impartiality, pronounces a final sentence, which all the cantons are obliged to enforce. We can gauge how well this arrangement works from a clause in their treaty of 1683 with Victor Amadeus of Savoy, in which he binds himself to step in as mediator in disputes between the cantons and, if necessary, to use force against the party that defies the ruling.

As far as their peculiar case can be compared with that of the United States, it confirms the principle I am trying to establish. Whatever effect the union may have had in ordinary cases, it failed the moment a difference arose that was strong enough to test it. The controversies over religion, which on three occasions set off violent and bloody conflicts, may be said in fact to have split the league. The Protestant and Catholic cantons have held separate diets since then, where all the most important business is settled, and they have left the general diet with little to do except look after the jointly held bailiwicks.

That separation had another consequence worth noting. It led to opposing alliances with foreign powers: Berne, at the head of the Protestant association, allied with the United Provinces, and Luzerne, at the head of the Catholic association, allied with France.
